body:
Two different ways to use Earth-observation information

Satellite observations become useful when users can find, view, interpret or obtain the information they need. Bhuvan and Bhoonidhi are both associated with the National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), an ISRO centre located in Hyderabad. Their main purposes, however, are different.

Bhuvan: Explore places and geographical information on maps.
Bhoonidhi: Search for and obtain Earth-observation satellite datasets.

Bhuvan: ISRO's Indian geo-platform

Bhuvan is ISRO's Indian geographical information platform. It allows users to explore satellite imagery and geographical information through mapping applications. Its services include 2D and 3D visualisation, thematic maps, and applications relevant to public administration and development.

A map becomes more informative when geographical layers are considered together. For instance, a satellite-image background may help a user understand the location of a settlement, while a thematic layer can provide information about water resources, agriculture or land use.

Important areas of Bhuvan application include:

  • Agriculture: Viewing geographical information relevant to agricultural areas.
  • Water resources: Exploring water-related maps and information.
  • Forestry: Using geographical information related to forest areas.
  • Rural and urban planning: Examining spatial information relevant to settlements and infrastructure.
  • Disaster management: Viewing available geographical information associated with hazards and their effects.

As a Gujarat-based example, a learner examining a district's settlements, water bodies and surrounding land can understand how satellite imagery and thematic geographical layers support local planning. This illustrates the type of task suited to Bhuvan; it does not imply that every type of local data is available for every district or date.

Connection with school geography

The Class 6 NCERT geography chapter on maps includes an activity using School Bhuvan-NCERT to draw a neighbourhood map over satellite imagery. The example connects ordinary map-reading concepts, such as location, direction and scale, with a practical Indian geospatial platform.

Although viewing and mapping are central to Bhuvan, it also provides access to selected downloadable data. It is therefore incorrect to say that Bhuvan can only display pictures and never provide data.

Bhoonidhi: ISRO's Earth Observation Data Hub

Bhoonidhi is an ISRO-NRSC platform for accessing Earth-observation satellite data. Its principal function is to help users search satellite-data archives and view, download or order available datasets.

A satellite dataset is more specific than the general geographical view seen on a map. It may be an observation acquired by a particular satellite sensor over a particular area and date. Such information matters when a user needs the underlying imagery or data for further study.

For example, a researcher studying how land cover changed between 2 dates may need appropriate satellite observations from those dates. Bhoonidhi is suited to searching for available scenes and obtaining the relevant data products.

Bhoonidhi includes data from Indian and selected foreign Earth-observation satellites. Depending on the dataset and its access conditions, a product may be available openly or may require ordering, payment or other permissions. It is not correct to assume that every dataset on the portal is free or immediately downloadable.

Bhoonidhi also offers data visualisation facilities, including Bhoonidhi VISTA. Thus, its primary identity as a data hub should not be converted into an absolute rule that it has no viewing functions.

Understanding the difference through a land-use example

Suppose an official wants to examine the geographical setting of a village. Viewing satellite imagery with relevant geographical layers is a task suited to Bhuvan.

Suppose a researcher instead needs satellite observations of that area acquired on particular dates for a land-cover comparison. Searching the observation archive and obtaining the datasets is a task suited to Bhoonidhi.

The difference is therefore primarily between using a geographical information platform and accessing source satellite data products. The capabilities overlap, but the main purposes remain distinct.

Prelims focus

  • Bhuvan is ISRO's Indian geo-platform.
  • Bhuvan supports satellite-image viewing, thematic mapping and geographical applications.
  • Bhoonidhi is ISRO's Earth Observation Data Hub.
  • Bhoonidhi supports searching, viewing, downloading and ordering satellite datasets.
  • Both are associated with NRSC, Hyderabad.
  • Trap: Bhuvan is not merely a raw-data archive, and Bhoonidhi is not merely a map-viewing website.

[References: NRSC-ISRO, Bhuvan: Indian Geo Platform of ISRO, sections Visualisation and Free Download, Application Sectors and Maps and OGC Services; NRSC-ISRO, Bhoonidhi Home, sections Bhoonidhi Browse and Order and Bhoonidhi VISTA; NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, chapter 4, Maps, printed p. 27, School Bhuvan-NCERT activity (official websites consulted 4 November 2026).]

pictures.caption: Bhuvan is centred on geographical exploration; Bhoonidhi helps users find specific satellite observations.

title: Bhuvan and Bhoonidhi: Mapping Information and Satellite Data

body:
Why specialised Earth-observation portals are needed

Earth-observation satellites provide measurements about different parts of the environment. A study of vegetation or land degradation requires different information from a study of clouds, rainfall or sea-surface temperature. ISRO provides specialised access to these kinds of information through platforms such as VEDAS and MOSDAC.

Both are associated with the Space Applications Centre (SAC) of ISRO, located in Ahmedabad, Gujarat. This is a direct Gujarat connection: an ISRO centre in Ahmedabad develops and provides access to space-derived information useful across India.

VEDAS: Visualisation of Earth Observation Data and Archival System

VEDAS stands for Visualisation of Earth Observation Data and Archival System. It is an ISRO-SAC platform that makes a wide range of information derived from Earth observations accessible for viewing and analysis.

VEDAS gives particular importance to thematic geospatial information. Thematic information describes a particular characteristic of a place rather than presenting only an unprocessed satellite image. It may relate to the condition of vegetation, land use, natural resources or environmental changes.

Examples of subjects supported by VEDAS include:

  • Vegetation and agriculture: Understanding spatial patterns associated with plant cover and agricultural areas.
  • Land use and land degradation: Studying the condition and changes of land over time.
  • Forests, wetlands and coastal resources: Exploring information relevant to natural-resource management.
  • Urban and environmental change: Examining how geographical patterns differ across places or periods.

VEDAS uses geographical data and analytical facilities to help users examine spatial patterns, meaning differences between locations, and temporal patterns, meaning changes over time.

For example, an environmental analyst might compare vegetation-related information for a region over different periods to identify changes. This illustrates VEDAS's emphasis on information derived from observations, rather than its being simply a catalogue of original satellite scenes.

The word Archival in VEDAS's full name does not make it identical to Bhoonidhi. VEDAS gives access to thematic and derived geospatial information and supports its use in analysis. Bhoonidhi's central role is discovering and obtaining satellite-observation datasets.

MOSDAC: Meteorological and Oceanographic Satellite Data Archival Centre

MOSDAC stands for Meteorological and Oceanographic Satellite Data Archival Centre. It is a data centre of ISRO's Space Applications Centre.

Meteorology concerns the atmosphere and weather. Oceanography concerns the physical and other characteristics of seas and oceans. MOSDAC is therefore concerned primarily with weather-related and ocean-related satellite observations and data products.

MOSDAC supports satellite-data reception, processing, analysis, archiving and dissemination. Examples of information associated with its subject area include:

  • Cloud observations: Information useful for examining cloud conditions.
  • Rainfall-related satellite products: Estimates and observations relevant to precipitation studies.
  • Sea-surface temperature: Information about temperature conditions at the ocean surface.
  • Atmospheric and marine conditions: Other available measurements relevant to weather and ocean studies.

These observations may support meteorological and oceanographic research and applications. However, a satellite-data portal should not be confused with an organisation that issues every official weather forecast or warning. MOSDAC's core role is to provide relevant data and products.

Gujarat examples

The distinction is useful when considering Gujarat's agriculture and coastline.

An analyst studying how vegetation conditions differ across agricultural regions could use relevant thematic information available through VEDAS. A researcher studying cloud patterns over Gujarat or sea-surface conditions in the Arabian Sea could look for appropriate meteorological or oceanographic satellite products through MOSDAC.

These are examples of suitable uses, not promises that a particular dataset, location or date will always be available on either platform.

Prelims focus

  • VEDAS: Visualisation of Earth Observation Data and Archival System.
  • VEDAS supports thematic geospatial information and its analysis, including land and natural-resource applications.
  • MOSDAC: Meteorological and Oceanographic Satellite Data Archival Centre.
  • MOSDAC supplies satellite-derived weather and ocean data products.
  • Both are associated with ISRO's Space Applications Centre in Ahmedabad, Gujarat.
  • Trap: VEDAS is not mainly an aviation-navigation service, and MOSDAC is not a satellite-navigation constellation.

[References: Space Applications Centre, ISRO, VEDAS, About Us, sections on thematic spatial data, natural resources and geospatial applications, page updated 13 August 2026; Space Applications Centre, ISRO, MOSDAC, About Us, sections on meteorological and oceanographic satellite-data reception, processing and dissemination, website reviewed 23 October 2026 (official websites consulted 4 November 2026).]

title: VEDAS and MOSDAC: Land, Weather and Ocean Information

body:
Identify the purpose before identifying the name

A reliable way to distinguish these 6 Indian space initiatives is to begin with the kind of information required. Position and time point towards satellite navigation. Maps, satellite datasets and environmental observations point towards Earth-observation information services.

Within these broad groups, the intended use provides the decisive distinction.

When the requirement concerns navigation

NavIC is the correct identification when the requirement is India's own regional navigation system, designed to provide positioning, navigation and timing. References to IRNSS, Standard Positioning Service and regional coverage around India also indicate NavIC.

GAGAN is the correct identification when the requirement is additional correction and integrity information for GPS, particularly to support civil aviation. References to AAI and satellite-based augmentation also indicate GAGAN.

When the requirement concerns Earth-observation information

Bhuvan is suited to exploring an area through satellite-image backgrounds, thematic geographical layers and mapping applications.

Bhoonidhi is suited to locating specific Earth-observation satellite datasets and obtaining available data products from an archive.

VEDAS is suited to exploring and analysing information derived from Earth observations, particularly thematic information concerning land, natural resources and environmental patterns.

MOSDAC is suited to obtaining information associated with satellite observations of weather and ocean conditions.

Commonly confused statements

Statement or clueCorrect interpretation
An Indian system is designed to determine position without relying on GPS.NavIC describes this independent regional-navigation design.
An Indian system provides integrity warnings and corrections for GPS.GAGAN is a GPS augmentation system.
A user wants to examine land and water information on a geographical map.Bhuvan is an appropriate mapping platform.
A researcher needs satellite observations acquired over an area on specified dates.Bhoonidhi is an appropriate Earth-observation data hub.
A user wants thematic information about vegetation or changing land conditions.VEDAS is an appropriate derived-information and analysis platform.
A user needs satellite products related to clouds or sea-surface temperature.MOSDAC is an appropriate weather-and-ocean data centre.

These matches describe the primary purposes of the initiatives. They do not imply that the platforms have no overlapping capabilities. For example, Bhuvan provides some downloadable data, Bhoonidhi provides visualisation facilities, and VEDAS covers several kinds of Earth-observation information.

Remember the institutional and geographical connections

  • ISRO: India's space agency associated with all 6 initiatives.
  • AAI: Jointly established GAGAN with ISRO and operates and maintains it.
  • NRSC, Hyderabad: Associated with Bhuvan and Bhoonidhi.
  • SAC, Ahmedabad: Associated with VEDAS and MOSDAC.

The Ahmedabad connection is especially relevant when studying science-and-technology institutions in Gujarat. It concerns a real ISRO centre and its work, rather than a geographical association invented from the subject matter of the portals.

Distinguish purpose, design and current status

Questions about a system's purpose are different from questions about its operational status on a specific date. NavIC remains India's independently designed regional navigation system even though the Department of Space reported on 29 July 2026 that it lacked the minimum 4 operational satellites for standalone positioning at that time.

Likewise, the launch of NVS-03 on 30 October 2026 is a confirmed event, but the ISRO update dated 31 October did not establish that the satellite had entered operational navigation service. A launch date should not be treated as proof of service availability.

For the other 4 portals, the core distinctions are comparatively stable: geographical mapping, satellite-data access, thematic Earth-observation analysis, and meteorological or oceanographic data access.

Prelims focus

  • NavIC: Independent regional-navigation architecture; positioning, navigation and timing.
  • GAGAN: GPS augmentation for civil aviation, including correction and integrity information.
  • Bhuvan: Geographical mapping and thematic visualisation.
  • Bhoonidhi: Earth-observation satellite-data discovery and access.
  • VEDAS: Thematic geospatial information and analysis; MOSDAC: Meteorological and oceanographic satellite data.
  • Trap: Do not confuse the original design of a constellation, a newly launched satellite and a confirmed operational navigation service.

[References: ISRO, FAQ Navigation, questions 1, 5, 15 and 16; ISRO, Satellite Navigation Services; NRSC-ISRO, Bhuvan Home and Bhoonidhi Home; Space Applications Centre, ISRO, VEDAS About Us and MOSDAC About Us; Department of Space, Parliamentary Question: Operational Status of NavIC Constellation, 29 July 2026; ISRO, Orbit Manoeuvring of NVS-03 Spacecraft, 31 October 2026 (official websites consulted 4 November 2026).]
